Inversions in parking functions

Kyle Celano CelanoDepartment of Mathematics, Wake Forest University, NC Email address: celanok@wfu.edu , Jennifer Elder ElderDepartment of Computer Science, Mathematics and Physics, Missouri Western State University, St. Joseph, MO 64507 Email address: jelder8@missouriwestern.edu , Kimberly P. Hadaway HadawayDepartment of Mathematics, Iowa State University, Ames, IA 50010 Email address: kph3@iastate.edu , Pamela E. Harris HarrisDepartment of Mathematical Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Milwaukee, WI 53211 Email address: peharris@uwm.edu , Amanda Priestley PriestleyDepartment of Computer Science, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712 Email address: amandapriestley@utexas.edu and Gabe Udell UdellDepartment of Mathematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14850 Email address: gru5@cornell.edu
Abstract.

In this paper, we obtain a qq-exponential generating function for inversions on parking functions via symmetric function theory and also through a direct bijection to rooted labeled forests. We then apply these techniques to unit interval parking functions to give analogous results. We conclude by introducing a probabilistic approach through which we obtain formulas for the total number of inversions and several other statistics across all parking functions and other sets of words closed under rearrangement.

1. Introduction

Throughout, let ℕ={1,2,…}\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,\dots\}, and if n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, then [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. Also, let 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} denote the set of permutations of [n][n]. Konheim and Weiss [30] defined parking functions as follows: consider a one-way street with nn parking spots (labeled in increasing order) and nn cars, each of which has a preferred spot. As each car parks, it drives to its preferred spot and parks there if it is unoccupied. If that spot is occupied, then the car continues driving and parks in the next available spot, if any exists. We encode the information of the preferred spots as a positive integer-valued preference list α=(α1,α2,…,αn)∈[n]n\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{n})\in[n]^{n}, where for each i∈[n]i\in[n], the positive integer αi\alpha_{i} indicates the preferred spot of car ii. We say the preference list α\alpha is a parking function if all cars are able to park using the aforementioned parking rule. The outcome permutation of α\alpha, denoted π⁡(α)\pi(\alpha), is defined by setting π​(α)​(i)=j\pi(\alpha)(i)=j if car jj parks in spot ii for each i∈[n]i\in[n]. We let PFn\PF_{n} be the set of all parking functions of length nn. Konheim and Weiss establish that the number of parking functions of length nn is (n+1)n−1(n+1)^{n-1}, see [30, Lemma 1]. A second proof of this count was given by Pollak by parking the cars on a circle with one new parking spot, see [16].

Introduced by Hadaway [25], a unit interval parking function of length nn is a parking function α∈PFn\alpha\in\PF_{n} such that π​(α)−1​(i)−αi≤1\pi(\alpha)^{-1}(i)-\alpha_{i}\leq 1 for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. In other words, these are parking functions in which, for all i∈[n]i\in[n], car ii parks either in its preference aia_{i} or in the spot after its preference ai+1a_{i}+1. Let UPFn\UPF_{n} denote the set of unit interval parking functions of length nn. Hadaway [25] proves that |UPFn|=Fubn|\UPF_{n}|=\Fub_{n}, which is the nt​hn^{th} Fubini number and counts the number of ordered set partitions of [n][n] [29, A000670]. Unit interval parking functions have been studied in connection to enumerating Boolean intervals of the weak Bruhat order of the symmetric group and in connection to the faces of the permutohedron [9, 13].

We are interested in the study of inversions of parking functions and unit interval parking functions. Recall that for a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, an inversion is a pair (i,j)(i,j) of integers in [n][n] such that i<ji<j and wi>wjw_{i}>w_{j}. We denote the set of inversions of a word ww by Inv⁡(w)\Inv(w) and let inv⁡(w)=|Inv⁡(w)|\inv(w)=|\Inv(w)|. Treating parking functions as words, for each n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we define the polynomials

PFn⁡(q)=∑α∈PFnqinv⁡(α)andUPFn⁡(q)=∑α∈UPFnqinv⁡(α),\PF_{n}(q)=\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}q^{\inv(\alpha)}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\UPF_{n}(q)=\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}q^{\inv(\alpha)},

and set PF0⁡(q)=UPF0⁡(q)=1\PF_{0}(q)=\UPF_{0}(q)=1. The inversion generating function PFn⁡(q)\PF_{n}(q) appeared incidentally in [37, Section 8] in their study of remixed Eulerian numbers and as we explain in Section 3, it appears as a specialization of certain symmetric functions studied in [28]. Beyond this, little has been said about inversions in parking functions directly.

Define

Expq⁡(z)=∑n≥0q(n2)​zn[n]q!and expq⁡(z)=∑n≥0zn[n]q!,\Exp_{q}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{\binom{n}{2}}\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!}\quad\mbox{and }\quad\exp_{q}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!},

where [n]q=1+q+⋯+qn−1[n]_{q}=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1} and [n]q!=[n]q[n−1]q⋯[1]q[n]_{q}!=[n]_{q}[n-1]_{q}\cdots[1]_{q}. With these definitions, using combinatorial techniques, we derive the following generating functions.

Theorem 1.1.

The qq-exponential generating functions for PFn⁡(q)\PF_{n}(q) and UPFn⁡(q)\UPF_{n}(q) are

∑n≥0PFn⁡(q)​zn+1[n]q!=(z​Expq⁡(−z))⟨−1⟩and ∑n≥0UPFn⁡(q)​zn[n]q!=12−expq⁡(z),\sum_{n\geq 0}\PF_{n}(q)\frac{z^{n+1}}{[n]_{q}!}=(z\Exp_{q}(-z))^{\langle-1\rangle}\quad\mbox{and }\quad\sum_{n\geq 0}\UPF_{n}(q)\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!}=\frac{1}{2-\exp_{q}(z)},

where F​(z)⟨−1⟩F(z)^{\langle-1\rangle} denotes the compositional inverse of F⁡(z)F(z).

Theorem 1.1 gives qq-analogues of classical results of Konheim and Weiss [30] and Cayley [7], respectively:

(1) ∑n≥0|PFn|​zn+1n!=(z​e−z)⟨−1⟩and ∑n≥0|UPFn|​znn!=12−ez,\sum_{n\geq 0}|\PF_{n}|\frac{z^{n+1}}{n!}=(ze^{-z})^{\langle-1\rangle}\quad\mbox{and }\quad\sum_{n\geq 0}|\UPF_{n}|\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\frac{1}{2-e^{z}},

where the latter result follows from the bijection between unit interval parking functions and Cayley permutations (see [25]). We also show that the equations in (1) follow from a more general theory of symmetric functions. The main result is as follows.

Theorem 1.2.

There are 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-modules ℂ⁡[PFn]\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}] and ℂ⁡[UPFn]\mathbb{C}[\UPF_{n}] such that

(2) ∑n≥0ch⁡ℂ⁡[PFn]​zn+1=(z​E​(−z))⟨−1⟩and ∑n≥0ch⁡ℂ⁡[UPFn]​zn=12−H⁡(z),\sum_{n\geq 0}\ch\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}]z^{n+1}=(zE(-z))^{\langle-1\rangle}\quad\mbox{and }\quad\sum_{n\geq 0}\ch\mathbb{C}[\UPF_{n}]z^{n}=\frac{1}{2-H(z)}\ ,

where ch\ch denotes the Frobenius characteristic map from 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-modules to symmetric functions of degree nn. Here, E⁡(z)=∑n≥0en​znE(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}e_{n}z^{n} and H⁡(z)=∑n≥0hn​znH(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}h_{n}z^{n} are generating functions for the elementary symmetric functions and the complete homogeneous symmetric functions, respectively.

The Frobenius image in (2) for parking functions was computed algebraically by Haiman [28]. In Section 3, we provide a new combinatorial proof using labeled rooted forests, which we construct in Section 2. Then, using a modified version of stable principal specialization, Theorem 1.2 gives a second proof of Theorem 1.1. For unit interval parking functions, we provide two ways of computing its Frobenius characteristic in Section 4: one by specializing a formula of Stanley and the other by more elementary arguments.

The study of the inversion statistic on PFn\PF_{n} and 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} has an important commonality: both set of words are 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant. Hence, we focus studying the average behavior of statistics in general on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant sets of words. With this approach in mind, in Section 5, we show that for any 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant subset W⊂ℕnW\subset\mathbb{N}^{n} of positive integers, we have a curious equality:

(3) ∑w∈Winv⁡(w)=n2​∑w∈Wdes⁡(w),\sum_{w\in W}\inv(w)=\frac{n}{2}\sum_{w\in W}\des(w),

where des⁡(w)\des(w) is the number of descents of ww i.e., the number of positions i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1] such that wi>wi+1w_{i}>w_{i+1}.

The intuition behind (3) involves noting that the total number of inversions can be written as the sum over all i<ji<j of the number of words with (i,j)(i,j) as an inversion. The key11 1 We credit Eyob Tsegaye for inspiring this approach. is to use the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action to move the positions (i,j)(i,j) to the positions (1,2)(1,2). Then, the probability that (i,j)(i,j) is an inversion is the same as the probability that (1,2)(1,2) is an inversion. Using a probabilistic perspective, one can utilize this observation to obtain (3). The idea of taking a statistic that is computed by summing over locations, computing the statistic by considering each location separately, and finally using 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariance of WW to move each location to the beginning, is a technique that applies more broadly. We introduce the notion of a kk-transitive function to describe the class of statistics that this argument applies to, and in Theorem 5.2 we give a vast generalization of (3). In Section 5.1, we explore applications of these ideas, and among our results we establish the results in Table 1. For the interested reader, Campion Loth, Levet, Liu, Stucky, Sundaram, and Yin [32] consider a similar problem for statistics on permutations in particular conjugacy classes.

2. Labeled rooted forests

The main objective of this section is to describe a statistic on rooted forests, which by way of a bijection to parking functions, maps to inversions of parking functions. We use standard definitions from graph theory for trees, forests, rooted trees, and rooted forests, for more on those topics we recommend [11]. To begin, recall that parking functions are in bijection with combinatorial objects called labeled rooted forests [30], where a rooted forest is made up of rooted trees in which every vertex is given a unique integer. We denote the set of labeled rooted forests on vertex set [n][n] by ℱn\F_{n}. If TT is a rooted labeled tree and vv is a nonroot vertex of TT, define the parent of vv, denoted p⁡(v)p(v), to be first element on the path from vv to the root of TT. We say that vv is a child of uu if p⁡(v)=up(v)=u. For a labeled rooted tree TT, let r⁡(T)r(T) denote its root. The subtrees of a labeled rooted tree TT are labeled rooted subtrees T1,T2,…,TkT_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{k} such that r⁡(Ti)r(T_{i}) is adjacent in TT to r⁡(T)r(T) for each i∈[k]i\in[k], where we order the trees so that r⁡(T1)<r⁡(T2)<⋯<r⁡(Tk)r(T_{1})<r(T_{2})<\cdots<r(T_{k}). An unlabeled rooted tree is called a rooted plane tree provided the children of each internal vertex are given a total ordering. A forest of rooted planar trees is a rooted plane forest if the forests are given a total ordering. Next, we introduce technical definitions used in our proofs.

Definition 2.1.

Let TT be a labeled rooted tree with root rr. The preorder traversal permutation w⁡(T)w(T) of TT is defined recursively by setting

w⁡(T)={r⁡(T)if T is the single vertex r⁡(T)r(T)⋅w(T1)⋅w(T2)⋯w(Tk)if T has subtrees T1,T2,…,Tk,w(T)=\begin{cases}r(T)&\text{if $T$ is the single vertex $r(T)$}\\ r(T)\cdot w(T_{1})\cdot w(T_{2})\cdots w(T_{k})&\text{if $T$ has subtrees $T_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{k}$},\end{cases}

where u⋅vu\cdot v denotes concatenation of words uu and vv.

For F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n}, define the preorder traversal permutation of FF to be the permutation w⁡(F)w(F) on {0}∪[n]\{0\}\cup[n] defined as follows: Suppose FF has trees T1,T2,…,TkT_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{k} with roots r1<r2<⋯<rkr_{1}<r_{2}<\cdots<r_{k}. Add a new vertex 0 to FF and connect the roots of T1,T2,…,TkT_{1},T_{2},\dots,T_{k} to 00 to make a rooted tree T⁡(F)T(F) rooted at 0. Then define wF=w⁡(T⁡(F))w_{F}=w(T(F)).

Françon [19] defines a bijection ρ:ℱn→PFn\rho:\F_{n}\to\PF_{n} by

(4) ρ⁡(F)=(wF−1​(p⁡(1)),wF−1​(p⁡(2)),…,wF−1​(p⁡(n))).\displaystyle\rho(F)=(w_{F}^{-1}(p(1)),w_{F}^{-1}(p(2)),\dots,w_{F}^{-1}(p(n))).

Figure 1 provides an example of ρ\rho, where, for instance, the entries in positions 3,10,3,10, and 1414 of ρ⁡(F)\rho(F) are each 22 because the nodes labeled 3,10,3,10, and 1414 in FF are the children of the node labeled 55, which is in position 22 of wFw_{F}.

Definition 2.2.

Suppose F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n}. The pair (i,j)(i,j) of integers i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] is called a parental preorder inversion of FF provided i<ji<j and wF−1​(p⁡(i))>wF−1​(p⁡(j))w_{F}^{-1}(p(i))>w_{F}^{-1}(p(j)). We denote the number of parental preorder inversions of FF by pinv⁡(F)\pinv(F).

For a vertex, ii, of a rooted labeled forest, FF, let p⁡(i)p(i) denote the parent of ii. Observe that (i,j)(i,j) is an inversion of ρ⁡(F)\rho(F) if and only if i<ji<j and wF−1​(p⁡(i))>wF−1​(p⁡(j))w_{F}^{-1}(p(i))>w_{F}^{-1}(p(j)). Hence, pinv⁡(F)=inv⁡(ρ⁡(F))\pinv(F)=\inv(\rho(F)) and thus we have shown:

Proposition 2.3.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, PFn⁡(q)=∑F∈ℱnqpinv⁡(F)\PF_{n}(q)=\displaystyle\sum_{F\in\F_{n}}q^{\pinv(F)}.

The constant term of PFn⁡(q)\PF_{n}(q) is the Catalan number Cn=1n+1​(2​nn)C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} [29, A000108] because on one hand the constant term is counting the weakly increasing plane forests and on the other hand, the constant term is counting unlabeled plane forests (see [53]).

3. Inversions in parking functions

In this section, we investigate inversions for parking functions by combining the bijection ρ:ℱn→PFn\rho:\F_{n}\to\PF_{n} with the classical parking function symmetric function of Haiman [28]. We assume a basic understanding of symmetric functions and 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-representation theory e.g. [51, Chapter 7] and [43].

We set the following notation for this and subsequent sections. A weak composition of nn with kk parts is a sequence (c1,c2,…,ck)(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k}) of nonnegative integers satisfying ∑i=1kci=n\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}=n. A composition is a weak composition with only positive parts. We let ℓ⁡(c)\ell(c) be the number of parts of a weak composition cc. Let Comp⁡(n,k)\Comp(n,k) and WComp⁡(n,k)\WComp(n,k) to be the set of compositions and weak compositions, respectively, of nn with kk parts. Also, let Comp⁡(n)=⋃kComp⁡(n,k)\Comp(n)=\bigcup_{k}\Comp(n,k) and likewise WComp⁡(n)=⋃kWComp⁡(n,k)\WComp(n)=\bigcup_{k}\WComp(n,k). Given a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} with largest value mm, the content of ww, denoted by con⁡(w)=(c1,c2,…,cm)∈WComp⁡(n)\con(w)=(c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{m})\in\WComp(n) is defined by setting cic_{i} to be the number of times the value ii appears in ww for each i∈[m]i\in[m].

Recall that the complete homogeneous symmetric function hch_{c} is defined by hc=hc1hc2⋯h_{c}=h_{c_{1}}h_{c_{2}}\cdots where for all positive integers kk, we have

hk≔∑1≤i1≤i2≤⋯≤ikxi1xi2⋯xik,h_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{1\leq i_{1}\leq i_{2}\leq\cdots\leq i_{k}}x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{k}},

and h0≔1h_{0}\coloneqq 1. Similarly, the elementary symmetric function ece_{c} is defined by ec=ec1ec2⋯e_{c}=e_{c_{1}}e_{c_{2}}\cdots, where for all positive integers kk, we have

ek≔∑1≤i1<i2<⋯<ikxi1xi2⋯xik,e_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}}x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\cdots x_{i_{k}},

and e0≔1e_{0}\coloneqq 1. Finally, the power-sum symmetric functions is defined by pc=pc1pc2⋯p_{c}=p_{c_{1}}p_{c_{2}}\cdots, where for all positive integers kk, we have

pk≔∑i≥1xik,p_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{i\geq 1}x_{i}^{k},

and p0≔1p_{0}\coloneqq 1.

If XX is a finite set, let ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] denote the vector space over ℂ\mathbb{C} with basis XX. If a group GG acts on XX, we abuse notation and let ℂ⁡[X]\mathbb{C}[X] also denote the standard GG-module defined by the action of GG on the basis XX (thus extending by linearity to the entire vector space). For an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module VV with character χ\chi, the Frobenius image is

ch⁡(V)=1n!​∑σ∈𝔖nχ⁡(σ)​pc​y​c​(σ),\ch(V)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\chi(\sigma)p_{cyc(\sigma)},

where c​y​c​(σ)cyc(\sigma) denotes the cycle type of σ\sigma. The map ch\ch from the set of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-modules to symmetric functions is called the Frobenius characteristic map.

Hence, this defines an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on ℱn\F_{n}. The map ρ\rho, defined in Equation 4, then extends to a map of vector spaces ρ:ℂ⁡[ℱn]→ℂ⁡[PFn]\rho:\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}]\to\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}] via linearity.

Recall that the area of α=(α1,α2,…,αn)∈PFn\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{n})\in\PF_{n} is the quantity

area⁡(α)=(n+12)−∑i=1nαi.\area(\alpha)=\binom{n+1}{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}.

Under the standard bijection of parking functions to labeled Dyck paths (see [61], page 54), the quantity area⁡(α)\area(\alpha) can be interpreted as the number of full squares below the Dyck path and above the main diagonal; see Figure 3.

Then, if PFn(i)\PF^{(i)}_{n} is the set of parking functions with area ii, ℂ⁡[PFn]\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}] has the structure of a graded module

ℂ⁡[PFn]=⨁i≥0ℂ⁡[PFn(i)].\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}]=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\mathbb{C}[\PF^{(i)}_{n}]\,.

Define the area of a rooted labeled forest F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n} as the quantity

area⁡(F)=(n+12)−∑i=1nwF−1​(p⁡(i)),\area(F)=\binom{n+1}{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}w^{-1}_{F}(p(i)),

and define the set

ℱn(i)={F∈ℱn∣area⁡(F)=i}.\F_{n}^{(i)}=\{F\in\F_{n}\mid\area(F)=i\}.

With these definitions at hand, we begin by establishing that ℂ⁡[ℱn]\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}] is a graded module.

Proposition 3.2.

The 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module ℂ⁡[ℱn]\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}] is a graded module

ℂ⁡[ℱn]=⨁i≥0ℂ⁡[ℱn(i)].\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}]=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}^{(i)}].

Moreover, the map ρ:ℂ⁡[ℱn]→ℂ⁡[PFn]\rho:\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}]\to\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}] is an isomorphism of graded 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-modules.

Proof.

Suppose ρ⁡(F)=α∈PFn\rho(F)=\alpha\in\PF_{n} for some F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n}, where ρ\rho is as in Equation 4. Let i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1]. If p⁡(i)=p⁡(i+1)p(i)=p(i+1), then wF−1​(p⁡(i))=wF−1​(p⁡(i+1))w_{F}^{-1}(p(i))=w_{F}^{-1}(p(i+1)), so (i,i+1)⋅ρ⁡(F)=ρ⁡(F)(i,i+1)\cdot\rho(F)=\rho(F). If p⁡(i)≠p⁡(i+1)p(i)\neq p(i+1), then wF−1​(p⁡(i))≠wF−1​(p⁡(i+1))w_{F}^{-1}(p(i))\neq w_{F}^{-1}(p(i+1)), so (i,i+1)⋅ρ⁡(F)=ρ⁡(si​(F))=ρ⁡(F)(i,i+1)\cdot\rho(F)=\rho(s_{i}(F))=\rho(F). Thus, for all σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, we have that ρ⁡(σ⋅F)=σ⋅ρ⁡(F)\rho(\sigma\cdot F)=\sigma\cdot\rho(F). Hence, ρ\rho is an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module isomorphism.

By definition of ρ\rho and the definitions of area on forests and parking functions, we have that area⁡(F)=area⁡(ρ⁡(F))\area(F)=\area(\rho(F)) for any F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n}. Since area⁡(α)=area⁡(σ⋅α)\area(\alpha)=\area(\sigma\cdot\alpha) for any α∈PFn\alpha\in\PF_{n} and for any σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, it follows that area⁡(F)=area⁡(ρ⁡(F))=area⁡(σ⋅ρ⁡(F))=area⁡(ρ⁡(σ⋅F))=area⁡(σ⋅F)\area(F)=\area(\rho(F))=\area(\sigma\cdot\rho(F))=\area(\rho(\sigma\cdot F))=\area(\sigma\cdot F). Hence, ℂ⁡[ℱn]\mathbb{C}[\F_{n}] is a graded 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module with grading given by area, and ρ\rho is a graded module isomorphism. ∎

Remark 3.3.

This parental preorder inversion statistic is not the usual statistic on ℱn\F_{n} that is related to the area on PFn\PF_{n}. An inversion of F∈ℱnF\in\F_{n} is a pair (i,j)(i,j) with 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n such that jj is an ancestor of ii. Let inv⁡(F)\inv(F) denote the number of inversions of FF. Kreweras [31] showed that inv\inv on ℱn\F_{n} is equidistributed with area\area on PFn\PF_{n}, meaning

∑α∈PFntarea⁡(α)=∑F∈ℱntinv⁡(F).\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}t^{\area(\alpha)}=\sum_{F\in\F_{n}}t^{\inv(F)}.

Hence, Proposition 3.2 shows that inv\inv on ℱn\F_{n} is equidistributed with area\area on ℱn\F_{n} i.e.,

(6) ∑F∈ℱntarea⁡(F)=∑F∈ℱntinv⁡(F).\sum_{F\in\F_{n}}t^{\area(F)}=\sum_{F\in\F_{n}}t^{\inv(F)}.

To prove this result bijectively, one could compose ρ\rho with the bijection of Kreweras. It would be of interest to have a direct bijection and we leave this an open problem.

Haiman provides a generating function formula for PFn⁡(𝐱)\PF_{n}(\mathbf{x}). To state it, begin by recalling the following generating functions:

3.2. Generating function formula for inversions on parking functions

The next ingredient in understanding inversions for parking functions is a general statement about words. For this, recall that the stable principal specialization of a symmetric function ff is defined to be

ps⁡(f)=f⁡(1,q,q2,…).\ps(f)=f(1,q,q^{2},\dots)\,.

In other words, we set xix_{i} to qi−1q^{i-1} for all i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

Next, for all nonnegative integers nn, define

(q;q)n≔(1−q)(1−q2)⋯(1−qn)=(1−q)n[n]q!.(q;q)_{n}\coloneqq(1-q)(1-q^{2})\cdots(1-q^{n})=(1-q)^{n}[n]_{q}!\,.

A set of length nn words W⊆ℕnW\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{n} is 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant if for all w∈Ww\in W and σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},

σ⋅w≔wσ−1​(1)wσ−1​(2)⋯wσ−1​(n)∈W.\sigma\cdot w\coloneqq w_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}w_{\sigma^{-1}(2)}\cdots w_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}\in W.

In other words, the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action σ⋅w\sigma\cdot w defined immediately above makes ℂ⁡[W]\mathbb{C}[W] an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module. There is a standard connection between stable principal specialization and inversion enumerators for words.

Proposition 3.5.

Let W⊆ℕnW\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{n} be an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words. Let F⁡(𝐱)F(\mathbf{x}) be the Frobenius image of the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module ℂ⁡[W]\mathbb{C}[W]. Then,

(q,q)n​ps⁡(F⁡(𝐱))=∑w∈Wqinv⁡(w).(q;q)_{n}\ps(F(\mathbf{x}))=\sum_{w\in W}q^{\inv(w)}.
Proof.

It is known [48, Equation 9.4], [22, Lemma 5.2] that for any composition α\alpha,

(q,q)n​ps⁡(hα)=[nα]q.(q;q)_{n}\ps(h_{\alpha})=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{\alpha}_{q}.

Recall that if w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} has content α\alpha and 𝔖n⋅w\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w denotes the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-orbit, then MacMahon [34] showed that

∑u∈𝔖n⋅wqinv⁡(u)=[nα]q.\sum_{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w}q^{\inv(u)}=\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{\alpha}_{q}.

Since the Frobenious image of ℂ⁡[𝔖n⋅w]\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w] is hαh_{\alpha}, the claim follows. ∎

Also for each nn, let Fn​(q)=∑w∈Wnqinv⁡(w)F_{n}(q)=\sum_{w\in W_{n}}q^{\inv(w)} be the inversion generating function for WnW_{n} and let Fn​(𝐱)F_{n}(\mathbf{x}) denote the Frobenius image of WnW_{n}. Then, we have

∑n≥1ps⁡(Fn​(𝐱))​zn​(1−q)n=∑n≥1Fn​(q)​zn[n]q!.\sum_{n\geq 1}\ps(F_{n}(\mathbf{x}))z^{n}(1-q)^{n}=\sum_{n\geq 1}F_{n}(q)\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!}\,.

Proof.

For n≥1n\geq 1, we have

ps⁡(Fn​(𝐱))​(z⁡(1−q))n=zn​(1−q)n​∑w∈W↑ps⁡(hcon⁡(w))=zn​(1−q)n​Fn​(q)(q,q)n=Fn​(q)​zn[n]q!,\ps(F_{n}(\mathbf{x}))(z(1-q))^{n}=z^{n}(1-q)^{n}\sum_{w\in W^{\uparrow}}\ps(h_{\con(w)})=z^{n}(1-q)^{n}\frac{F_{n}(q)}{(q;q)_{n}}=F_{n}(q)\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!},

∑n≥0PFn⁡(q)​zn+1[n]q!=(z​Expq⁡(−z))⟨−1⟩.\sum_{n\geq 0}\PF_{n}(q)\frac{z^{n+1}}{[n]_{q}!}=(z\Exp_{q}(-z))^{\langle-1\rangle}.

ps⁡(E⁡(z⁡(1−q)))=∑n≥0ps⁡(en)​zn​(1−q)n=∑n≥0q(n2)(q,q)n​zn​(1−q)n=∑n≥0q(n2)​zn[n]q!=Expq⁡(z).\ps(E(z(1-q)))=\sum_{n\geq 0}\ps(e_{n})z^{n}(1-q)^{n}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{(q;q)_{n}}z^{n}(1-q)^{n}=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{\binom{n}{2}}\frac{z^{n}}{[n]_{q}!}=\Exp_{q}(z)\,.

4. Inversions in unit interval parking functions

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈PFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\PF_{n}. As in [5], we call α\alpha a unit interval parking function if every car parks in its preference or in the spot after its preference and write α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n}. In Section 4.1, we begin our study by providing a bijection between the set of unit interval parking functions and the set of Cayley permutations, which have appeared in the literature under various names. In Section 4.2, we give a generating function for the number of inversions in unit interval parking functions. In Section 4.3, we conclude with some related symmetric function results.

4.1. A connection to Cayley permutations

We begin by providing a connection between Cayley permutations and unit interval parking functions. A Cayley permutation of length nn is a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that if ii appears in ww, then each j∈[i]j\in[i] also appear in ww. We denote the set of all Cayley permutations of length nn by ℭn\mathfrak{C}_{n}. Cayley permutations of length nn can be equivalently characterized as the set ℭn={w∈[n]n:con⁡(w)∈Comp⁡(n)}\C_{n}=\{w\in[n]^{n}:\con(w)\in\Comp(n)\}. Cayley permutations appear in the literature under various names, including Fubini words, packed words, surjective words, and initial words [35, 36]. We note that Cayley permutations have also been viewed as ordered set partitions, and descent generating functions for Cayley permutations have been studied in [8]. Refined counts of ordered set partitions have been studied before but in different contexts; see Remark 4.5 for further details.

First, we need an important characterization of unit interval parking functions. Let β\beta be the weakly increasing rearrangement of α\alpha and suppose {i∈[n]∣βi=i}={i1<i2<⋯<ik}\{i\in[n]\mid\beta_{i}=i\}=\{i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}\}. Then, the block structure [5, Definition 2.7] of α\alpha is a decomposition of α\alpha into blocks π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πk\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{k} of strings defined by

πj=βijβij+1⋯βij+1−1\pi_{j}=\beta_{i_{j}}\beta_{i_{j}+1}\cdots\beta_{i_{j+1}-1}

for each j∈[k]j\in[k]. This is also called the prime decomposition of α\alpha in [9, Remark 2.7].

The following result establishes that a unit interval parking function is uniquely determined by its block sizes and the positions of its blocks.

Theorem 4.1 ([5, Theorem. 2.9]).

Let α=(a1,a2,…,an)∈UPFn\alpha=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\UPF_{n} and let α↑=(a1′,a2′,…,an′)\alpha^{\uparrow}=(a^{\prime}_{1},a_{2}^{\prime},\dots,a^{\prime}_{n}) be the weakly increasing rearrangement of α\alpha. Then:

  1. (1)

    ai′∈{i,i+1}a^{\prime}_{i}\in\{i,i+1\} for all ii.

  2. (2)

    Place a separator in α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} before each element ai′a^{\prime}_{i} satisfying ai′=ia^{\prime}_{i}=i, we obtain a decomposition α↑=π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πm\alpha^{\uparrow}=\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{m}, where each πj\pi_{j} is of the form (i,i,i+1,i+2,…,i+j)(i,i,i+1,i+2,\dots,i+j). The words πj\pi_{j} are called the blocks of α\alpha.

  3. (3)

    The sizes of the blocks determine α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} uniquely.

  4. (4)

    The entries in each block appear in increasing order in α\alpha. Equivalently, a rearrangement σ\sigma of α\alpha is in UPFn\UPF_{n} if and only if the entries in σ\sigma respect the relative order of the entries in each block πj\pi_{j}.

  5. (5)

    In particular, the number of UPFs with increasing rearrangement α↑\alpha^{\uparrow} is (n|π1|,|π2|,…,|πm|)\binom{n}{|\pi_{1}|,|\pi_{2}|,\ldots,|\pi_{m}|}.

Next, we utilize Theorem 4.1 to establish a bijection between unit interval parking functions and Cayley permutations.

Lemma 4.2.

Define ψ:UPFn→ℭn\psi:\UPF_{n}\to\C_{n} as follows: suppose α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n} has block-structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πk\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{k}. Let αi\alpha_{i} denote the iith entry of α\alpha, and ψ​(α)i\psi(\alpha)_{i} denote the iith entry of ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha). Set

ψ​(α)i=j if αi appears in πj\psi(\alpha)_{i}=j\quad\text{ if $\alpha_{i}$ appears in $\pi_{j}$}

for each i∈ni\in n. Then ψ\psi is a bijection such that for all α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n}, Inv⁡(ψ⁡(α))=Inv⁡(α)\Inv(\psi(\alpha))=\Inv(\alpha).

Proof.

First, the image of ψ\psi is indeed a Cayley permutation since the numbers 1,2,…,k1,2,\dots,k appear at least once each in ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) if α\alpha has kk blocks.

Suppose α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n} and αi>αj\alpha_{i}>\alpha_{j} for some i<ji<j. By Theorem 4.1 part (4), αi\alpha_{i} is in a strictly larger (indexed) block than αj\alpha_{j}. Hence, ψ​(α)i>ψ​(α)j\psi(\alpha)_{i}>\psi(\alpha)_{j}. On the other hand, if αi≤αj\alpha_{i}\leq\alpha_{j} for some i<ji<j, then αi\alpha_{i} and αj\alpha_{j} are either in the same block, or αi\alpha_{i} is in a smaller (indexed) block than αj\alpha_{j}. Hence, ψ​(α)i≤ψ​(α)j\psi(\alpha)_{i}\leq\psi(\alpha)_{j}. Thus, Inv⁡(ψ⁡(α))=Inv⁡(α)\Inv(\psi(\alpha))=\Inv(\alpha).

Suppose ψ⁡(α)=ψ⁡(β)\psi(\alpha)=\psi(\beta). Then, we can see that α\alpha and β\beta must have the same block structure since the contents of ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) and ψ⁡(β)\psi(\beta) are the same. By definition, ψ​(α)i=ψ​(β)i=j\psi(\alpha)_{i}=\psi(\beta)_{i}=j if an element of block πj\pi_{j} appears in position ii of α\alpha and β\beta. By Theorem 4.1 part (4), there is only one way to arrange the elements of each block πj\pi_{j} such that an element of πj\pi_{j} appears in the positions ii such that ψ​(α)i=j\psi(\alpha)_{i}=j. Hence, α=β\alpha=\beta.

Given a Cayley permutation w∈ℭnw\in\C_{n}, let c=con⁡(w)=(c1,c2,…,ck)c=\con(w)=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k}) be the content of ww. For each j∈[k]j\in[k], if i1<i2<⋯<icji_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{c_{j}} are the positions of the jj’s in ww, then replace the j′​sj^{\prime}s (from left to right) by a,a,a+1,a+2,…,a+cj−1a,a,a+1,a+2,\dots,a+c_{j}-1, where a=c1+c2+⋯+cj−1+1a=c_{1}+c_{2}+\cdots+c_{j-1}+1 to construct a sequence α\alpha (where we set c0=0c_{0}=0). The sequence α\alpha is proven to be a unit interval parking function in the proof of [5, Theorem 2.5]. Moreover, ψ⁡(α)=w\psi(\alpha)=w since the block structure of α\alpha is cc. ∎

where we recall that ℓ⁡(c)\ell(c) denotes the number of parts of a weak composition cc. Since every weak composition can be made by adding 0’s to a (strong) composition, we have

∑c∈WComp⁡(n)[nc1,c2,…,cℓ⁡(c)]q⋅12ℓ⁡(c)=∑c∈Comp⁡(n)[nc1,c2,…,cℓ⁡(c)]q​∑j≥0(ℓ⁡(c)+jj)​12ℓ⁡(c)+j.\displaystyle\sum_{c\in\WComp(n)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{c_1,c_2,\dots,c_{\ell(c)}}_{q}\cdot\frac{1}{2^{\ell(c)}}=\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}\genfrac{[}{]}{0.0pt}{}{n}{c_1,c_2,\dots,c_{\ell(c)}}_{q}\sum_{j\geq 0}\binom{\ell(c)+j}{j}\frac{1}{2^{\ell(c)+j}}.

Expanding 2−(m+1)​(1−x)−(m+1)2^{-(m+1)}(1-x)^{-(m+1)} with Newton’s generalized binomial theorem and then substituting x=1/2x=1/2, we have that for all positive integers mm,

∑j≥0(m+jj)​12m+j+1=1.\sum_{j\geq 0}\binom{m+j}{j}\frac{1}{2^{m+j+1}}=1.

Hence, the claim follows. ∎

Remark 4.5.

The definition of UPFn⁡(q)\UPF_{n}(q) along with the closed form in Theorem 4.4 make it a compelling qq-analog of Fubn\Fub_{n}. However, there is a different qq-analog of Fubn\Fub_{n}, which has received much more attention in the literature. Originally studied under the name ROS\operatorname{ROS} by Steíngrimsson [55], an “inversion,” as defined by Remmel and Wilson [40], of a ordered set partition B=(B1,…,Bk)B=(B_{1},\dots,B_{k}) is pair (i,Bj)(i,B_{j}) such that ii appears in an earlier block than BjB_{j} and ii is greater than something in BjB_{j}. This kind of inversion has been related to the Delta Conjecture, an important conjecture in the theory of symmetric functions [26]. This “inversion” statistic has been shown to be equidistributed with a number of other statistics, and the resulting qq-analog has many wonderful properties [26, 41, 27]. The Delta Conjecture context is also closely related to parking functions, leading us to wonder whether it is coincidence that ordered set partitions can be viewed as parking functions themselves.

4.3. Unit interval parking function symmetric function

To generalize to a result on symmetric functions, we require an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on UPFn\UPF_{n}. Suppose α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n} has block structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πk\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{k}, as described in Theorem 4.1. For i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1], define

(i,i+1)⋅α={αif αi,αi+1 are in the same block(α1,α2,…,αi−1,αi+1,αi,αi+2,…,αn)if αi,αi+1 are in different blocks.(i,i+1)\cdot\alpha=\begin{cases}\alpha&\text{if $\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+1}$ are in the same block}\\ (\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{i-1},\alpha_{i+1},\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+2},\dots,\alpha_{n})&\text{if $\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+1}$ are in different blocks.}\end{cases}

One can check that this defines an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on UPFn\UPF_{n}, as noted in [9, pg. 11]. The content of α\alpha is the composition

con⁡(α)=(|π1|,|π2|,…,|πk|).\con(\alpha)=(|\pi_{1}|,|\pi_{2}|,\dots,|\pi_{k}|).

In [5, Theorem 2.9], the authors show that two unit interval parking functions have the same content if and only if they are rearrangements of each other. Moreover, they show that for each composition c∈Comp⁡(n)c\in\Comp(n) there is a unit interval parking function α\alpha with con⁡(α)=c\con(\alpha)=c. Thus,

UPFn⁡(𝐱)=∑c∈Comp⁡(n)hc.\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}h_{c}.

Since UPFn\UPF_{n} and ℭn\C_{n} have the same Frobenius image, they are isomorphic as 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-modules. In particular, we show that the map ψ\psi, defined in Lemma 4.2, is an explicit isomorphism.

Proposition 4.6.

Let ψ:UPFn→ℭn\psi:\UPF_{n}\to\C_{n} be as in Lemma 4.2. Then, for all α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n}, con⁡(ψ⁡(α))=con⁡(α)\con(\psi(\alpha))=\con(\alpha). Moreover, ψ\psi extends to an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module isomorphism.

Proof.

For α∈UPFn\alpha\in\UPF_{n} with block structure π1|π2​∣⋯∣​πk\pi_{1}\mid\pi_{2}\mid\cdots\mid\pi_{k}, The map ψ\psi replaces each element of block πj\pi_{j} with a jj for each j∈[k]j\in[k]. Hence, entry jj of con⁡(α)=(|π1|,|π2|,…,|πk|)\con(\alpha)=(|\pi_{1}|,|\pi_{2}|,\dots,|\pi_{k}|) is exactly the number of jj’s in ψ⁡(α)\psi(\alpha) for each j∈[k]j\in[k], so con⁡(α)=con⁡(ψ⁡(α))\con(\alpha)=\con(\psi(\alpha)).

Suppose i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1]. If αi\alpha_{i} and αi+1\alpha_{i+1} are in the same block, then ψ​(α)i=ψ​(α)i+1\psi(\alpha)_{i}=\psi(\alpha)_{i+1}. Hence, (i,i+1)⋅ψ⁡(α)=ψ⁡(α)=ψ⁡((i,i+1)⋅α)(i,i+1)\cdot\psi(\alpha)=\psi(\alpha)=\psi((i,i+1)\cdot\alpha). On the other hand, if αi\alpha_{i} and αi+1\alpha_{i+1} are in different blocks, then ψ​(α)i≠ψ​(α)i+1\psi(\alpha)_{i}\neq\psi(\alpha)_{i+1}, so

(i,i+1)⋅ψ⁡(α)=(ψ​(α)1,ψ​(α)2,…,ψ​(α)i−1,ψ​(α)i+1,ψ​(α)i,ψ​(α)i+2,…,ψ​(α)n)=ψ⁡((i,i+1)⋅α).(i,i+1)\cdot\psi(\alpha)=(\psi(\alpha)_{1},\psi(\alpha)_{2},\dots,\psi(\alpha)_{i-1},\psi(\alpha)_{i+1},\psi(\alpha)_{i},\psi(\alpha)_{i+2},\dots,\psi(\alpha)_{n})=\psi((i,i+1)\cdot\alpha).

Hence, ψ\psi is an isomorphism of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-actions. ∎

Theorem 4.7.

We have ∑n≥0UPFn⁡(𝐱)​zn=12−H⁡(z)\sum_{n\geq 0}\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x})z^{n}=\frac{1}{2-H(z)}, where H⁡(z)H(z) is defined in Equation 8.

Proof.

The result follows by writing

12−H⁡(z)=∑k≥012k+1​(∑n≥0hn​zn)k=∑n≥0zn​∑c∈Comp⁡(n)hc​∑j≥0(ℓ⁡(c)+jj)​12ℓ⁡(c)+j+1\frac{1}{2-H(z)}=\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}h_{n}z^{n}\right)^{k}=\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}h_{c}\sum_{j\geq 0}\binom{\ell(c)+j}{j}\frac{1}{2^{\ell(c)+j+1}}

and recalling that ∑j≥0(ℓ⁡(c)+jj)​12ℓ⁡(c)+j+1=1\sum_{j\geq 0}\binom{\ell(c)+j}{j}\frac{1}{2^{\ell(c)+j+1}}=1. ∎

While setting t=2t=2 makes sense for polynomials, it is not clear what the representation theoretic meaning is of this evaluation. In particular, we do not know how to derive Theorem 4.7 from a known 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-representation on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}.

Just like ℂ⁡[PFn]\mathbb{C}[\PF_{n}], ℂ⁡[UPFn]\mathbb{C}[\UPF_{n}] is a graded 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module, with the grading coming from the area function, the function

UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)≔∑α∈UPFn↑tarea⁡(α)​hcon⁡(α)\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t)\coloneqq\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}^{\uparrow}}t^{\area(\alpha)}h_{\con(\alpha)}

is the graded Frobenius image of ℂ⁡[UPFn]\mathbb{C}[\UPF_{n}]. This means that

UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)=∑k=0n−1ch⁡(ℂ⁡{α∈UPFn∣area⁡(α)=k})​tk.\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\ch\left(\mathbb{C}\{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}\mid\area(\alpha)=k\}\right)t^{k}.

We can likewise get a nice expression for the generating function of UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t).

Theorem 4.8.

The generating function of UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t) is

∑n≥0UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)​zn=t[2]t−H⁡(t​z)\sum_{n\geq 0}\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t)z^{n}=\frac{t}{[2]_{t}-H(tz)}
Proof.

We first rewrite the right-hand side as

t[2]t−H⁡(t​z)=t(t+1)−H⁡(t​z)=11−H⁡(t​z)−1t\frac{t}{[2]_{t}-H(tz)}=\frac{t}{(t+1)-H(tz)}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{H(tz)-1}{t}}

and note that

H⁡(t​z)−1=∑n≥1hn​zn​tn.H(tz)-1=\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{n}z^{n}t^{n}.

Then, we have

11−H⁡(t​z)−1t\displaystyle\frac{1}{1-\frac{H(tz)-1}{t}} =∑k≥01tk​(∑n≥1hn​zn​tn)k\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{1}{t^{k}}\left(\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{n}z^{n}t^{n}\right)^{k}
=∑n≥0zn​∑c∈Comp⁡(n)tn−ℓ⁡(c)​hc.\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}t^{n-\ell(c)}h_{c}.

Now we just have to show that

UPFn⁡(𝐱,t)=∑c∈Comp⁡(n)tn−ℓ⁡(c)​hc.\UPF_{n}(\mathbf{x},t)=\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}t^{n-\ell(c)}h_{c}.

Indeed, observe that if α∈UPFn↑\alpha\in\UPF_{n}^{\uparrow} and con⁡(α)=(c1,c2,…,cn−k)\con(\alpha)=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{n-k}), then for each i∈[n−k]i\in[n-k], cars 2+∑j=1i−1cj,3+∑j=1i−1cj,…,ci+∑j=1i−1cj2+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}c_{j},3+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}c_{j},\dots,c_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}c_{j} each park exactly 1 spot away from their preference, and thus contribute ci−1c_{i}-1 in total to the area. Thus, area⁡(α)=c1+c2+⋯+cn−k−(n−k)=k\area(\alpha)=c_{1}+c_{2}+\dots+c_{n-k}-(n-k)=k, and so we have the desired expression. ∎

5. Expectations of kk-transitive statistics

In this section, we continue our discussion on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant sets of words by connecting the total number of inversions on the set to the total number of descents in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words. The parking function motivation comes from Schumacher’s [46, Theorem 10] which establishes

(22) ∑α∈PFndes⁡(α)=(n2)​(n+1)n−2.\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\des(\alpha)=\binom{n}{2}(n+1)^{n-2}.

Using probabilistic techniques, we obtain an analogous formula for inversions on parking functions, which we state and prove in Corollary 5.4. Moreover, we extend this to a larger class of statistics on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words, namely those defined via kk-transitive functions.

For a random variable f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} on a finite set Ω\Omega, define the expectation of ff with respect to the uniform measure on Ω\Omega to be

(23) 𝔼Ω⁡[f]=1|Ω|​∑x∈Ωf⁡(x)=∑y∈ℝℙΩ​(f=y)⋅y,\E_{\Omega}[f]=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{x\in\Omega}f(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}(f=y)\cdot y,

where we denote the discrete uniform probability distribution by

ℙΩ​(f=y)=|{x∈Ω∣f⁡(x)=y}||Ω|.\mathbb{P}_{\Omega}(f=y)=\frac{|\{x\in\Omega\mid f(x)=y\}|}{|\Omega|}.

For further definitions and background in probability, see [12, 15, 24]. When we know the size of a set and our random variables are chosen appropriately, computing the expectation of a statistic (23) is equivalent to computing the sum of the statistic over the elements of the set. We use the language of expected value to clarify combinatorial arguments which would otherwise be much more cumbersome. Linearity of expectation and symmetry often lie at the heart of these arguments. In the same way that descents are inversions that happen next to each other, we can consider ‘adjacent’ and ‘non-adjacent’ versions of other statistics. In Theorem 5.2, we prove a general result relating expectations (and therefore counts) of such pairs of statistics. Our first application is to obtain the total number of inversions of parking functions from Schumacher’s count of the total number of descents. In Section 5.1, we explore numerous other applications of this.

For positive integers k≤nk\leq n, define the set

In,k={(i1,i2,…,ik)∣1≤i1<i2<⋯<ik≤n}.I_{n,k}=\{(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k})\mid 1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{k}\leq n\}.

A function χ:ℕn×In,k→ℝ\chi:\mathbb{N}^{n}\times I_{n,k}\to\mathbb{R} is said to be kk-transitive provided there is a function θ:ℕk→ℝ\theta:\mathbb{N}^{k}\to\mathbb{R} such that

(24) χ⁡(w,(i1,i2​…,ik))=θ⁡(wi1,wi2,…,wik)\chi(w,(i_{1},i_{2}\dots,i_{k}))=\theta(w_{i_{1}},w_{i_{2}},\dots,w_{i_{k}})

for each w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} and (i1,i2,…,ik)∈In,k(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k})\in I_{n,k}. In other words, χ\chi depends only on the ordered list of values wi1,wi2,…,wikw_{i_{1}},w_{i_{2}},\dots,w_{i_{k}} and not on the positions. The name comes from the fact that the symmetric group 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} acts kk-transitively on [n][n] for any k∈[n]k\in[n], meaning if p=(i1,i2,…,ik)\textbf{p}=(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}) and q=(j1,j2,…,jk)\textbf{q}=(j_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{k}) are a vector of distinct values of [n][n], then there is a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that σ⁡(is)=js\sigma(i_{s})=j_{s} for all s∈[k]s\in[k]. Moreover, if χ\chi is kk-transitive, then

(25) χ⁡(w,p)=χ⁡(σ⋅w,q)\chi(w,\textbf{p})=\chi(\sigma\cdot w,\textbf{q})

for any w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}.

Let WW be a finite subset of ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} and let χ\chi be a kk-transitive function. Define random variables on WW by setting

(26) fχ​(w)=∑p∈In,kχ⁡(w,p)andgχ​(w)=∑i=0n−kχ⁡(w,(1+i,2+i,…,k+i))f_{\chi}(w)=\sum_{\textbf{p}\in I_{n,k}}\chi(w,\textbf{p})\quad\text{and}\quad g_{\chi}(w)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}\chi(w,(1+i,2+i,\dots,k+i))

for all w∈Ww\in W. We start by giving an example of a transitive function that both serves as a motivation as well as being of interest in what follows.

Example 5.1.

Let WW be a finite subset of ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. For w∈Ww\in W and integers 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n, define

χinv​(w,(i,j))={1wi>wj0wi≤wj.\chi^{\inv}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w_{i}>w_{j}\\ 0&w_{i}\leq w_{j}.\end{cases}

We can see that χinv\chi^{\inv} is a 22-transitive function with θ⁡(a,b)=1\theta(a,b)=1 if a>ba>b, and 00 if a≤ba\leq b. In the language of probability, χinv\chi^{\inv} is a classical example of an indicator random variable. Moreover, fχinvf_{\chi^{\inv}} is the classical inversion statistic inv\inv, while gχinvg_{\chi^{\inv}} is the classical descent statistic des\des.

For W=PFnW=\PF_{n}, we can rephrase (22) as a statement about the expectation 𝔼PFn⁡[des]=𝔼PFn⁡[gχinv]\E_{\PF_{n}}\left[\des\right]=\E_{\PF_{n}}\left[g_{\chi^{\inv}}\right] of the random variable gχinvg_{\chi^{\inv}} on PFn\PF_{n}. Analogously, we want to compute the expectation 𝔼PFn⁡[inv]\E_{\PF_{n}}\left[\inv\right] of inv=fχinv\inv=f_{\chi^{\inv}}. Note that the probabilistic interpretation of these computations is to determine the expected number of decents (or inversions) in a uniformly random parking function of length nn.

For a kk-transitive function χ\chi, define a restriction

χ1​(w)≔χ⁡(w,(1,2,…,k))\chi_{1}(w)\coloneqq\chi(w,(1,2,\dots,k))

for w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. For instance, if χ=χinv\chi=\chi^{\inv}, then χ1inv​(w)=1\chi^{\inv}_{1}(w)=1 if ww has a descent in position 1 and is 0 otherwise.

Theorem 5.2.

Let k≤nk\leq n be positive integers. Let χ:ℕn×In,k→ℝ\chi:\mathbb{N}^{n}\times I_{n,k}\to\mathbb{R} be a kk-transitive function and let W⊆ℕnW\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{n} be an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words. With fχf_{\chi} and gχg_{\chi} as in Equation 26, we have

  1. (1)

    𝔼W⁡[fχ]=(nk)​𝔼W​[χ1]\E_{W}[f_{\chi}]=\binom{n}{k}\E_{W}[\chi_{1}],

  2. (2)

    𝔼W⁡[gχ]=(n−k+1)​𝔼W​[χ1]\E_{W}[g_{\chi}]=(n-k+1)\E_{W}[\chi_{1}], and

  3. (3)

    𝔼W⁡[fχ]=1k​(nk−1)​𝔼W​[gχ]\E_{W}[f_{\chi}]=\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\E_{W}[g_{\chi}].

Proof.

For a fixed element p=(i1,i2,…,ik)∈In,k\textbf{p}=(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k})\in I_{n,k}, fix σ\sigma to be a permutation such that σ⁡(is)=s\sigma(i_{s})=s for each s∈[k]s\in[k]. Since WW is 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant, for all w∈Ww\in W we have

σ⋅w=(wσ−1​(1),wσ−1​(2),…,wσ−1​(n))∈W.\sigma\cdot w=(w_{\sigma^{-1}(1)},w_{\sigma^{-1}(2)},\dots,w_{\sigma^{-1}(n)})\in W.

Since χ\chi is kk-transitive, we can use Equation 25 with q=(1,2,…,k)\textbf{q}=(1,2,\dots,k) to get that for any y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}

ℙW​(χ⁡(w,p)=y)=ℙW​(χ1​(σ⋅w)=y)=ℙW​(χ1​(u)=y),\mathbb{P}_{W}(\chi(w,\textbf{p})=y)=\mathbb{P}_{W}(\chi_{1}(\sigma\cdot w)=y)=\mathbb{P}_{W}(\chi_{1}(u)=y),

where σ\sigma is the permutation such that σ⁡(is)=s\sigma(i_{s})=s for all s∈[k]s\in[k]. Therefore, by linearity of expectation, we have

(27) 𝔼W​[fχ]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{W}\left[f_{\chi}\right] =∑p∈In,k𝔼W​[χ⁡(w,p)]=∑p∈In,k𝔼W⁡[χ1]=(nk)​𝔼W​[χ1],\displaystyle=\sum_{\textbf{p}\in I_{n,k}}\mathbb{E}_{W}\left[\chi(w,\textbf{p})\right]=\sum_{\textbf{p}\in I_{n,k}}\E_{W}[\chi_{1}]=\binom{n}{k}\E_{W}[\chi_{1}],

since |In,k|=(nk)|I_{n,k}|=\binom{n}{k}, proving (a).

For part (b), we proved in part (a) that ℙW​(χ⁡(w,(i,i+1,…,i+k−1)=y)=ℙW​(χ1​(w)=y)CLOSE\mathbb{P}_{W}\left(\chi(w,(i,i+1,\dots,i+k-1)=y\right)=\mathbb{P}_{W}\left(\chi_{1}(w)=y\right) for all i∈[n−k]i\in[n-k]. Hence,

𝔼W⁡[gχ]=∑i=1n−k+1𝔼W⁡[χ⁡(w,(i,i+1,…,i+k−1))]=(n−k+1)​𝔼W​[χ1],\E_{W}\left[g_{\chi}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n-k+1}\E_{W}\left[\chi(w,(i,i+1,\dots,i+k-1))\right]=(n-k+1)\E_{W}[\chi_{1}],

as desired.

Finally, part (c) follows from combining (a) and (b). ∎

By selecting χ\chi to be the 2-transitive function χinv\chi^{\inv} and by the definition of expectation applied to indicator random variables, we immediately obtain the following.

Corollary 5.3.

Let W⊂ℕnW\subset\mathbb{N}^{n} be an 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words of positive integers. Then,

  1. (a)

    𝔼W⁡[inv]=(n2)​ℙW​(χ1inv=1)\E_{W}\left[\inv\right]=\binom{n}{2}\mathbb{P}_{W}\left(\chi^{\inv}_{1}=1\right),

  2. (b)

    𝔼W⁡[des]=(n−1)​ℙW​(χ1inv=1)\E_{W}\left[\des\right]=(n-1)\mathbb{P}_{W}\left(\chi^{\inv}_{1}=1\right), and

  3. (c)

    𝔼W⁡[inv]=n2​𝔼W​[des]\E_{W}\left[\inv\right]=\frac{n}{2}\E_{W}\left[\des\right].

Note that part (c) of Corollary 5.3 is equivalent to

(28) ∑w∈Winv⁡(w)=n2​∑w∈Wdes⁡(w).\sum_{w\in W}\inv(w)=\frac{n}{2}\sum_{w\in W}\des(w).

From this, we can therefore derive the desired analogue of Schumacher’s result (22) for inversions since PFn\PF_{n} is 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant.

Corollary 5.4.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the total number of inversions across all parking functions is

∑α∈PFninv⁡(α)=n​(n+1)n−22​(n2).\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\inv(\alpha)=\frac{n(n+1)^{n-2}}{2}\binom{n}{2}.

Let Fubn=|ℭn|\Fub_{n}=|\C_{n}| be the nn-th Fubini number defined by

Fubn=∑k=0n∑j=0k(−1)k−j​(kj)​jn.\Fub_{n}=\sum_{{k=0}}^{n}\sum_{{j=0}}^{k}(-1)^{{k-j}}{\binom{k}{j}}j^{n}.

The sequence of Fubini numbers is OEIS sequence A000670. We obtain similar results for unit interval parking functions.

Corollary 5.5.

Let n≥1n\geq 1.

  1. (1)

    The total number of descents across all unit interval parking functions, (or equivalently all Cayley permutations) is

    ∑α∈UPFndes⁡(α)=n−12​(Fubn−Fubn−1).\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}\des(\alpha)=\frac{n-1}{2}(\Fub_{n}-\Fub_{n-1}).
  2. (2)

    The total number of inversions across all unit interval parking functions, (or equivalently all Cayley permutations) is

    ∑α∈UPFninv⁡(α)=n⁡(n−1)4​(Fubn−Fubn−1).\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}\inv(\alpha)=\frac{n(n-1)}{4}(\Fub_{n}-\Fub_{n-1}).
Proof.

By Lemma 4.2, we can work with Cayley permutations.

First observe that

ℙℭn​(χ1inv=1)=ℙℭn​(α1>α2)=ℙℭn​(α1<α2)=12​(1−ℙℭn​(α1=α2)).\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\chi_{1}^{\inv}=1)=\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\alpha_{1}>\alpha_{2})=\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2})=\frac{1}{2}(1-\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2})).

The map

{α∈ℭn∣α1=α2}→ℭn−1,\{\alpha\in\C_{n}\mid\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}\}\rightarrow\C_{n-1},

defined by α=(α1,α2,α3,…,αn)↦(α2,α3,…,αn)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},\dots,\alpha_{n})\mapsto(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3},\dots,\alpha_{n}) is a bijection, so we have

(29) ℙℭn​(α1=α2)=|ℭn−1||ℭn|=Fubn−1Fubn,\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2})=\frac{|\C_{n-1}|}{|\C_{n}|}=\frac{\Fub_{n-1}}{\Fub_{n}},

and thus

(30) 𝔼ℭn⁡(χ1inv)=ℙℭn​(χ1inv=1)=Fubn−Fubn−12​Fubn.\E_{\C_{n}}(\chi_{1}^{\inv})=\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\chi_{1}^{\inv}=1)=\frac{\Fub_{n}-\Fub_{n-1}}{2\Fub_{n}}.

Applying Corollary 5.3 part (b) to (30) we get

∑α∈UPFndes⁡(α)\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}\des(\alpha) =Fubn⁡𝔼ℭn⁡[des]\displaystyle=\Fub_{n}\E_{\C_{n}}[\des]
=Fubn⁡(n−1)​ℙℭn​(χ1inv=1)\displaystyle=\Fub_{n}(n-1)\mathbb{P}_{\C_{n}}(\chi_{1}^{\inv}=1)
(31) =n−12​(Fubn−Fubn−1).\displaystyle=\frac{n-1}{2}(\Fub_{n}-\Fub_{n-1}).

Applying Corollary 5.3 part (c) to (31) yields

∑α∈UPFninv⁡(α)=n⁡(n−1)4​(Fubn−Fubn−1).∎\sum_{\alpha\in\UPF_{n}}\inv(\alpha)=\frac{n(n-1)}{4}(\Fub_{n}-\Fub_{n-1}).\qed
Remark 5.6.

Theorem 5.2 is a statement about any finite 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant set of words W⊂ℕnW\subset\mathbb{N}^{n}, so perhaps it is of interest to view the result as a statement about the 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-module ℂ⁡[W]\mathbb{C}[W] or about its Frobenius image. However, it is unclear at this time what the representation theoretic significance is.

The only property of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} used in Theorem 5.2 is that it acts kk-transitively on [n][n]. Thus, we have the following generalization.

Proposition 5.7.

Let k≤nk\leq n be positive integers. Let GG be a group that acts kk-transitively on [n][n] and let W⊂ℕnW\subset\mathbb{N}^{n} be a GG-invariant set of words of positive integers. For any kk-transitive function χ:ℕn×In,k→ℝ\chi:\mathbb{N}^{n}\times I_{n,k}\to\mathbb{R}, we have

  1. (1)

    𝔼W⁡[fχ]=(nk)​𝔼W⁡(χ1)\E_{W}[f_{\chi}]=\binom{n}{k}\E_{W}(\chi_{1}),

  2. (2)

    𝔼W⁡[gχ]=(n−k+1)​𝔼W⁡(χ1)\E_{W}[g_{\chi}]=(n-k+1)\E_{W}(\chi_{1}), and

  3. (3)

    𝔼W⁡[fχ]=1k​(nk−1)​𝔼W⁡(gχ)\E_{W}[f_{\chi}]=\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\E_{W}(g_{\chi}).

Example 5.8.

Let 𝔖n+\mathfrak{S}_{n}^{+} denote the alternating subgroup of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Then using the work of Désarménien and Foata [10], Fulman et al. in [21, Eqn. (7)]) note that if An​(q)=∑w∈𝔖nqdes⁡(w)A_{n}(q)=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}q^{\des(w)}, then

∑π∈𝔖2​n+qdes⁡(π)=2​A2​n​(q)+(1−q)n​An​(q)and∑π∈𝔖2​n+1+qdes⁡(π)=2​A2​n+1​(q)+(1−q)n​An+1​(q).\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n}^{+}}q^{\des(\pi)}=2A_{2n}(q)+(1-q)^{n}A_{n}(q)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n+1}^{+}}q^{\des(\pi)}=2A_{2n+1}(q)+(1-q)^{n}A_{n+1}(q).

Considering both equations separately, we take a derivative with respect to qq of both sides and set q=1q=1, to arrive at

(32) ∑π∈𝔖2​n+des⁡(π)=2​∑π∈𝔖2​ndes⁡(π)and∑π∈𝔖2​n+1+des⁡(π)=2​∑π∈𝔖2​n+1des⁡(π).\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n}^{+}}\des(\pi)=2\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n}}\des(\pi)\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n+1}^{+}}\des(\pi)=2\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{2n+1}}\des(\pi).

We give more details on the history and counts of descents and inversions in permutations at the start of the next section, and use those counts along with the equations in (32) to determine that

(33) ∑π∈𝔖n+des⁡(π)=12​∑π∈𝔖ndes⁡(π)=n!​(n−1)4.\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}^{+}_{n}}\des(\pi)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\des(\pi)=\frac{n!(n-1)}{4}.

Since the alternating group 𝔖n+\mathfrak{S}_{n}^{+} acts 2-transitively on [n][n] for n≥4n\geq 4, we can conclude by Proposition 5.7 that

(34) ∑π∈𝔖n+inv⁡(π)=n!​n​(n−1)8.\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}^{+}_{n}}\inv(\pi)=\frac{n!n(n-1)}{8}.

As a consequence, one can also see that total number of descents or inversions is the same in 𝔖n∖𝔖n+\mathfrak{S}_{n}\setminus\mathfrak{S}_{n}^{+} as there is in 𝔖n+\mathfrak{S}_{n}^{+}. The equality of the total number of descents can be shown combinatorially via the involution of Wachs [60].

5.1. Applications

The method of enumerating statistics by way of computing the expectation of a carefully chosen kk-transitive function has numerous applications. In particular, one can apply Theorem 5.2 straightforwardly in the following scenarios to obtain results, both old and new.

5.1.1. Inversions and descents in permutations

Counting the total number of inversions [29, A001809] is a very old problem from 1838 posed by Stern [57] and solved by Terquem [59]. The sequence enumerating the total number of descents is known as the Lah numbers [29, A001286]. Note we used these results in Example 5.8, now we prove them independently by using Corollary 5.3.

Corollary 5.9.

The number of descents and inversions in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} is given by

∑w∈𝔖ndes⁡(w)=n!​(n−1)2and∑w∈𝔖ninv⁡(w)=n2​n!​(n−1)2=n!​n​(n−1)4,\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\des(w)=\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\inv(w)=\frac{n}{2}\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}=\frac{n!n(n-1)}{4},

respectively.

Proof.

Recall that χinv:ℕn×In,2→{0,1}\chi^{\inv}:\mathbb{N}^{n}\times I_{n,2}\to\{0,1\} is defined by

χinv​(w,(i,j))={1wi>wj0wi≤wj,\chi^{\inv}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w_{i}>w_{j}\\ 0&w_{i}\leq w_{j}\,,\\ \end{cases}

and that this has fχinv=invf_{\chi^{\inv}}=\inv and gχinv=desg_{\chi^{\inv}}=\des. For w∈𝔖nw\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, the probability that χinv​(w,(1,2))=1\chi^{\inv}(w,(1,2))=1 is exactly 12\frac{1}{2}. Hence, by Corollary 5.3 part (b), we have that

𝔼𝔖n⁡[des]=(n−1)​12.\E_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}[\des]=(n-1)\frac{1}{2}\,.

Thus, we have

∑w∈𝔖ndes⁡(w)=n!​(n−1)2.\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\des(w)=\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}.

In an analogous fashion, applying Corollary 5.3 part (c) yields

∑w∈𝔖ninv⁡(w)=n2​n!​(n−1)2=n!​n​(n−1)4.\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\inv(w)=\frac{n}{2}\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}=\frac{n!n(n-1)}{4}.

∎

5.1.2. Ties in words

A tie in a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} is a position ii such that wi=wi+1w_{i}=w_{i+1}. The number of ties of ww is denoted tie⁡(w)\tie(w). We have the following application of the aforementioned technique.

Corollary 5.10.

Let ww be a word with content (c1,c2,…,cℓ)(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{\ell}). Then

∑u∈𝔖n⋅wtie⁡(u)=2n​∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ).\sum_{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w}\tie(u)=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}\,.
Proof.

Define

χtie​(w,(i,j))={1wi=wj0wi≠wj.\chi^{\tie}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w_{i}=w_{j}\\ 0&w_{i}\neq w_{j}.\end{cases}

Then, tie⁡(w)=gχtie​(w)\tie(w)=g_{\chi^{\tie}}(w). If con⁡(w)=(c1,c2,…,cℓ)\con(w)=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{\ell}), then

fχtie​(w)=(c12)+(c22)+⋯+(cℓ2)f_{\chi^{\tie}}(w)=\binom{c_{1}}{2}+\binom{c_{2}}{2}+\cdots+\binom{c_{\ell}}{2}

as this function simply selects pairs of numbers which are the same. If W=𝔖n⋅wW=\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w, then |W|=(nc1,c2,…,cℓ)|W|=\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{\ell}} and fχtie​(u)=fχtie​(w)f_{\chi^{\tie}}(u)=f_{\chi^{\tie}}(w) for all u∈Wu\in W, so

∑u∈𝔖n⋅wfχtie​(u)=(nc1,c2,…,cℓ)⁡((c12)+⋯+(cℓ2))=∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ).\sum_{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w}f_{\chi^{\tie}}(u)=\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{\ell}}\left(\binom{c_{1}}{2}+\cdots+\binom{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}.

Thus, the total number of ties is

∑u∈𝔖n⋅wtie⁡(u)=2n​∑u∈𝔖n⋅wfχtie​(u)=2n​∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ).∎\sum_{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w}\tie(u)=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\cdot w}f_{\chi^{\tie}}(u)=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}.\qed

For some particular choices of WW, Corollary 5.10 has interesting interpretations. In particular, we are able to derive nicer formulas for the total number of ties across all Cayley permutations (Proposition 5.11) and across all parking functions (Corollary 5.14), leading us to wonder if there exist bijective proofs that the formulas we can derive from Corollary 5.10 are equal to these simpler expressions.

Proposition 5.11.

The total number of ties across all Cayley permutations of length nn is

∑w∈ℭntie⁡(w)=(n−1)​Fubn−1.\sum_{w\in\C_{n}}\tie(w)=(n-1)\Fub_{n-1}.
Proof.

This follows from Equation 29, which says that

𝔼ℭn⁡[χ1tie]=|ℭn−1||ℭn|=Fubn−1Fubn,\E_{\C_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{\tie}]=\frac{|\C_{n-1}|}{|\C_{n}|}=\frac{\Fub_{n-1}}{\Fub_{n}},

where Fubn\Fub_{n} denotes the nn-th Fubini number. ∎

Combining Proposition 5.11 with Corollary 5.10, yields the identity

2n​∑c∈Comp⁡(n)∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ)=(n−1)​Fubn−1.\frac{2}{n}\sum_{c\in\Comp(n)}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}=(n-1)\Fub_{n-1}\,.

Finding a bijective proof of this fact remains an open problem; see Section 6 for a formal statement.

Remark 5.12.

If Fub⁡(z)=∑n≥0Fubn⁡zn/n!\Fub(z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\Fub_{n}z^{n}/n!, then recall that Fub⁡(z)=12−ez\Fub(z)=\frac{1}{2-e^{z}} and thus

Fub⁡(z)′=∑n≥1Fubn⁡zn−1(n−1)!=∑n≥2(n−1)​Fubn−1​zn−2(n−1)!=∑n≥1(∑α∈ℭntie⁡(α))​zn−2(n−1)!\Fub(z)^{\prime}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\Fub_{n}\frac{z^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=\sum_{n\geq 2}(n-1)\Fub_{n-1}\frac{z^{n-2}}{(n-1)!}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\C_{n}}\tie(\alpha)\right)\frac{z^{n-2}}{(n-1)!}

by Proposition 5.11. Since Fub⁡(z)=(2−ez)−1\Fub(z)=(2-e^{z})^{-1}, we have

∑n≥1(∑α∈ℭntie⁡(α))​zn−2(n−1)!=(12−ez)=ez(2−ez)2.\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{\alpha\in\C_{n}}\tie(\alpha)\right)\frac{z^{n-2}}{(n-1)!}=\left(\frac{1}{2-e^{z}}\right)=\frac{e^{z}}{(2-e^{z})^{2}}.

Hence,

∑n≥0(∑w∈ℭn+1tie⁡(w))​znn!=z​ez(2−ez)2.\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(\sum_{w\in\C_{n+1}}\tie(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\frac{ze^{z}}{(2-e^{z})^{2}}.

For parking functions, as with Cayley permutations, we can get a nice formula for the total number of ties without invoking Corollary 5.10.

Lemma 5.13.

The number of parking functions of length nn having a tie in position 1 is given by

(n+1)n−2.(n+1)^{n-2}\,.
Proof.

We begin by recalling the map of Pollak [42]: Given a sequence (w1,w2,…,wn)∈[n+1]n(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[n+1]^{n}, we can imagine cars parking on a circular street with n+1n+1 spots with preference list ww. Since there are nn cars and n+1n+1 spots, there is empty spot. If ii is the empty spot, set

α=(w1−i,w2−i,…,wn−i),\alpha=(w_{1}-i,w_{2}-i,\dots,w_{n}-i),

where all entries are taken modulo n+1n+1. This defines a parking function α∈PFn\alpha\in\PF_{n} and hence an (n+1)(n+1)-to-1 map ψ:[n+1]n→PFn\psi:[n+1]^{n}\to\PF_{n} as proven in [16]. Then we can see that ψ⁡(w)\psi(w) is a parking function with a tie in position 1 if and only if ww has a tie in position 11. Since there are (n+1)n−1(n+1)^{n-1} sequences w∈[n+1]nw\in[n+1]^{n} such that ww has a tie in position 1, and since ψ\psi is (n+1)(n+1)-to-1, we have

|{α∈PFn∣α1=α2}|=(n+1)n−1n+1=(n+1)n−2.∎|\{\alpha\in\PF_{n}\mid\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}\}|=\frac{(n+1)^{n-1}}{n+1}=(n+1)^{n-2}.\qed

As a consequence of Theorem 5.2, we have the following.

Corollary 5.14.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

∑α∈PFntie⁡(α)=(n−1)​(n+1)n−2.\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\tie(\alpha)=(n-1)(n+1)^{n-2}.
Remark 5.15.

Corollary 5.14 can also be derived from [46, Theorem 13] which says that if PF(n,i)\PF_{(n,i)} is the set of parking functions with ii ties, then

|PF(n,i)|=(n−1i)​nn−1−i.|\PF_{(n,i)}|=\binom{n-1}{i}n^{n-1-i}.

Hence, we have

∑α∈PFntie⁡(α)=∑i=0n−1i​(n−1i)​nn−1−i=(n−1)​∑i=1n−1(n−2i−1)​nn−1−i=(n−1)​(n+1)n−2,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\tie(\alpha)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}i\binom{n-1}{i}n^{n-1-i}=(n-1)\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\binom{n-2}{i-1}n^{n-1-i}=(n-1)(n+1)^{n-2},

where the final equality is an application of the binomial theorem.

By Schumacher’s result on the number of ties, we can write Corollary 5.14 as

(35) ∑α∈PFndes⁡(α)=n2​∑α∈PFntie⁡(α).\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\des(\alpha)=\frac{n}{2}\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\tie(\alpha).

The equality in (35) does not hold in general for all 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant sets of words. For example, the equality ∑w∈Wdes⁡(w)=n2​∑w∈Wtie⁡(w)\sum_{w\in W}\des(w)=\frac{n}{2}\sum_{w\in W}\tie(w) does not hold when W=𝔖nW=\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Thus, we can apply Theorem 5.2 to conclude that

∑α∈PFndes⁡(α)=∑α∈PFnfχtie​(α).\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\des(\alpha)=\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}f_{\chi^{\tie}}(\alpha).

This indicates that there is a bijection

{(α,i)∣α∈PFn,i∈Des(α)}→{(α,(r,s))∣α∈PFn,1≤r<s≤n,αr=αs}.\{(\alpha,i)\mid\alpha\in\PF_{n},i\in\Des(\alpha)\}\to\{(\alpha,(r,s))\mid\alpha\in\PF_{n},1\leq r<s\leq n,\alpha_{r}=\alpha_{s}\}.

We leave it as an open problem to find this bijection explicitly in Section 6.

To get a formula for the number of ties across all parking functions using Corollary 5.10, we recall that parking functions can be described as the collection of words in [n]n[n]^{n} whose content con⁡(w)=(c1,c2,…,cn)\con(w)=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{n}) satisfies

(36) i≤c1+c2+⋯+ci≤n,i\leq c_{1}+c_{2}+\cdots+c_{i}\leq n,

for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Let Hess⁡(n)\mathrm{Hess}(n) denote the set of sequences (c1,c2,…,cn)(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{n}) of nonnegative integers satisfying Equation 36.22 2 The notation comes from literature of “Hessenberg functions” which are functions h:[n]→[n]h:[n]\to[n] satisfying i≤h⁡(i)i\leq h(i) for all i∈[n]i\in[n] and h⁡(i)≤h⁡(i+1)h(i)\leq h(i+1) for all i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1]. These functions are a central object in the work on chromatic quasisymmetric functions of Shareshian and Wachs [48]. Then we may apply Corollary 5.10 and 5.14 to establish the following.

Corollary 5.16.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

∑c∈Hess⁡(n)∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ)=(n2)​(n+1)n−2.\sum_{c\in\mathrm{Hess}(n)}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}=\binom{n}{2}(n+1)^{n-2}.

We again leave it as an open problem to find this bijection explicitly, and state this formally in Section 6.

5.1.3. Descent tops and inversion tops

Recall that the major index of a permutation ww is maj⁡(w)=∑i∈Des⁡(w)i\maj(w)=\sum_{i\in\Des(w)}i, or the sum of the indices where a decent occurs in ww. This can be thought of as summing over descents weighted by the position they occur in. Instead of weighting by position, we can weight by its value and arrive at the descent top statistic defined by

dtop⁡(w)=∑i∈Des⁡(w)wi.\dtop(w)=\sum_{i\in\Des(w)}w_{i}.

For sequence data on the descent top statistic see A263753. For a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, define

χdtop​(w,(i,j))={wiwi>wj0else,\chi^{\dtop}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}w_{i}&w_{i}>w_{j}\\ 0&\text{else,}\end{cases}

The function χdtop\chi^{\dtop} is a 22-transitive function and dtop=gχdtop\dtop=g_{\chi^{\dtop}}. We can also define the inversion top statistic as

fχdtop​(w)=itop⁡(w)=∑i<jχdtop​(w,(i,j)).f_{\chi^{\dtop}}(w)=\itop(w)=\sum_{i<j}\chi^{\dtop}(w,(i,j)).

For r∈[n]r\in[n], the probability that χdtop​((w,(1,2))=rCLOSE\chi^{\dtop}((w,(1,2))=r is 1n​r−1n−1\frac{1}{n}\frac{r-1}{n-1} because you need to select a permutation with w1=rw_{1}=r and w2<rw_{2}<r. Hence, we have

𝔼𝔖n⁡[χ1dtop]\displaystyle\E_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{\dtop}] =∑r=1nr−1n⁡(n−1)⋅r\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r-1}{n(n-1)}\cdot r
=1n⁡(n−1)​∑r=1nr2−r\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^{2}-r
=1n⁡(n−1)​(n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6−n⁡(n+1)2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\left(\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)
=n+13.\displaystyle=\frac{n+1}{3}.

Thus, we have

(37) ∑w∈𝔖ndtop⁡(w)=(n+1)!​(n−1)3∑w∈𝔖nitop⁡(w)=(n+1)!​n​(n−1)6=(n+13)​n!.\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\dtop(w)=\frac{(n+1)!(n-1)}{3}\qquad\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\itop(w)=\frac{(n+1)!n(n-1)}{6}=\binom{n+1}{3}n!.

5.1.4. Graphical inversions

Let DD be a directed graph on vertex set [n][n] and directed edge set EE, the elements of which we represent using arrows i→j∈Ei\to j\in E. For a word w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n}, define

χD​(w,(i,j))={1wi→wj∈E0wi→wj∉E.\chi^{D}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w_{i}\to w_{j}\in E\\ 0&w_{i}\to w_{j}\not\in E.\end{cases}

If we define θ⁡(x,y)=1\theta(x,y)=1 if x→y∈Ex\to y\in E and 00 otherwise for x,y∈[n]x,y\in[n], then χD​(w,(i,j))=θ⁡(wi,wj)\chi^{D}(w,(i,j))=\theta(w_{i},w_{j}) for all w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n}, so this is a 22-transitive function. The function fχDf_{\chi^{D}} is the graphical inversion statistic, denoted invD′\inv_{D}^{\prime}, studied by Foata and Zeilberger in [18], where it was studied alongside the analogously defined graphical major index We have

(38) 𝔼𝔖n⁡[χ1D]=|E|n⁡(n−1)\E_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{D}]=\frac{|E|}{n(n-1)}

since χ1D​(w)=1\chi^{D}_{1}(w)=1 if and only if w1→w2∈Ew_{1}\to w_{2}\in E for each w∈𝔖nw\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Defining the graphical descent statistic as desD′=gχD\des_{D}^{\prime}=g_{\chi^{D}}, we have

(39) ∑w∈𝔖ninvD′⁡(w)=n!​(n2)​|E|n⁡(n−1)=n!​|E|2and∑w∈𝔖ndesD′⁡(w)=n!​(n−1)​|E|n⁡(n−1)=(n−1)!​|E|.\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\inv_{D}^{\prime}(w)=n!\binom{n}{2}\frac{|E|}{n(n-1)}=\frac{n!|E|}{2}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\des_{D}^{\prime}(w)=n!(n-1)\frac{|E|}{n(n-1)}=(n-1)!|E|.

by combining Equation 38 with Theorem 5.2.

If we take DD to be the complete graph with edges of the form i→ji\to j whenever i>ji>j, we have χD=χinv\chi^{D}=\chi^{\inv} and |E|=(n2)|E|=\binom{n}{2} is the number of edges, so Equation 39 yield the formulas in Corollary 5.9.

5.1.5. Descents, big and small

Instead of looking at all inversions, we can restrict our attention to inversions of a particular form. For a word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, indices ii and jj define

χsdes​(w,(i,j))={1w⁡(i)=w⁡(j)+10else.\chi^{\sdes}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w(i)=w(j)+1\\ 0&\text{else.}\end{cases}

Then we define sdes=gχsdes\sdes=g_{\chi^{\sdes}} which counts the number of small descents of ww, i.e., positions ii where w⁡(i)=w⁡(i+1)+1w(i)=w(i+1)+1, and likewise sinv=fχsdes\sinv=f_{\chi^{\sdes}} counts small inversions, i.e., positions i<ji<j where w⁡(i)=w⁡(j)+1w(i)=w(j)+1. Observe that if σ\sigma is a permutation, then

(40) sinv⁡(σ)=des⁡(σ−1)\sinv(\sigma)=\des(\sigma^{-1})

and so

(41) ∑σ∈𝔖nsinv⁡(σ)=∑σ∈𝔖ndes⁡(σ)=n!​(n−1)2.\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\sinv(\sigma)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\des(\sigma)=\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}.

One advantage of using sinv⁡(σ)\sinv(\sigma) over des⁡(σ−1)\des(\sigma^{-1}) is that the former is more easily generalizable to words.

We can also define big descents and big inversions as bdes=gχbdes\bdes=g_{\chi^{\bdes}} and binv=fχbdes\binv=f_{\chi^{\bdes}}, respectively, where

χbdes​(w,(i,j))={1w⁡(i)>w⁡(j)+10else.\chi^{\bdes}(w,(i,j))=\begin{cases}1&w(i)>w(j)+1\\ 0&\text{else.}\end{cases}

for a given word w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n} and pair 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n. Note that χinv=χsdes+χbdes\chi^{\inv}=\chi^{\sdes}+\chi^{\bdes}. Big descents correspond to 11-descents of Foata and Schutzenberger [17]. These were more recently studied by Shareshian and Wachs in a quasisymmetric function generalization of Eulerian polynomials [47, 48] and by Elizalde, Rivera, Zhuang on sets of pattern avoiding permutations [14]. To compute expectations, note that a permutation starting with a small descent starts with a number ii bigger than 11 and then i−1i-1. Thus, it follows that

(42) 𝔼𝔖n⁡[χ1sdes]=(n−1)⋅1n⁡(n−1)=1n=1−𝔼𝔖n⁡[χ1bdes].\E_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{\sdes}]=\frac{(n-1)\cdot 1}{n(n-1)}=\frac{1}{n}=1-\E_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{\bdes}].

Thus, combining Equation 42 and Theorem 5.2 (or equivalently Equation 41, Theorem 5.2, and Corollary 5.9), we have the following.

Proposition 5.17.

Suppose n≥1n\geq 1.

  1. (1)

    ∑σ∈𝔖nsdes⁡(w)=(n−1)​(n−1)!\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\sdes(w)=(n-1)(n-1)!.

  2. (2)

    ∑σ∈𝔖nsinv⁡(w)=(n2)⁡(n−1)!=n!​(n−1)2\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\sinv(w)=\binom{n}{2}(n-1)!=\frac{n!(n-1)}{2}.

  3. (3)

    ∑σ∈𝔖nbdes⁡(w)=(n−1)​(n−2)​(n−1)!2\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\bdes(w)=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)(n-1)!}{2}.

  4. (4)

    ∑σ∈𝔖nbinv⁡(w)=(n−1)​(n−2)​n!4\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\binv(w)=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)n!}{4}.

Items (1) and (3) appear to be well-known; see A001563 and A001804, respectively.

For parking functions, the statistic sinv\sinv counts the number of pairs of cars with adjacent preferences ii and i+1i+1 so that the second car has the smaller preference. Similarly, sdes\sdes counts the number of pairs of adjacent cars, car ii and car i+1i+1, with adjacent preferences jj and j−1j-1, respectively.

The Pollak map [n+1]n→PFn[n+1]^{n}\to\PF_{n} (discussed in Lemma 5.13) sends w=(a1,…,an)w=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) to a parking function α\alpha of the form (a1−i,…,an−i)(a_{1}-i,\dots,a_{n}-i) for some ii, where the subtraction is computed modulo n+1n+1. If χ1sdes​(α)=1\chi_{1}^{\sdes}(\alpha)=1, then a1−i=a2−i+1(modn+1)a_{1}-i=a_{2}-i+1\pmod{n+1}, so we must have that a1−a2=1(modn+1)a_{1}-a_{2}=1\pmod{n+1} On the other hand, If w1=w2+1w_{1}=w_{2}+1 or w1=1w_{1}=1 and w2=nw_{2}=n, then i∉{w1,w2}i\not\in\{w_{1},w_{2}\} since both w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} must be occupied, so χ1sdes​(α)=1\chi_{1}^{\sdes}(\alpha)=1. Hence, α\alpha has χ1sdes​(α)=1\chi_{1}^{\sdes}(\alpha)=1 if and only if a1−a2=1(modn+1)a_{1}-a_{2}=1\pmod{n+1}. For w=(a1,a2,…,an)∈W=[n+1]n,w=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in W=[n+1]^{n}, the probability a1−a2=1(modn+1)a_{1}-a_{2}=1\pmod{n+1} is 1n+1\frac{1}{n+1} since the first letter can be freely chosen and the second letter is uniquely determined by the first, so

(43) 𝔼PFn⁡[χ1sdes]=1n+1.\E_{\PF_{n}}[\chi_{1}^{\sdes}]=\frac{1}{n+1}.

Thus, combining Equation 43 and Theorem 5.2, we have the following.

Proposition 5.18.

Let n≥1n\geq 1.

  1. (1)

    ∑w∈PFnsdes⁡(w)=(n−1)​(n+1)n−2\sum_{w\in\PF_{n}}\sdes(w)=(n-1)(n+1)^{n-2} .

  2. (2)

    ∑w∈PFnsinv⁡(w)=(n2)​(n+1)n−2\sum_{w\in\PF_{n}}\sinv(w)=\binom{n}{2}(n+1)^{n-2}.

  3. (3)

    ∑w∈PFnbdes⁡(w)=(n−12)​(n+1)n−2\sum_{w\in\PF_{n}}\bdes(w)=\binom{n-1}{2}(n+1)^{n-2}.

  4. (4)

    ∑w∈PFnbinv⁡(w)=n⁡(n−1)​(n−2)​(n+1)n−24\sum_{w\in\PF_{n}}\binv(w)=\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)^{n-2}}{4}.

5.1.6. Permutation patterns

We finish our probabilistic discussion with a closer look at when W=𝔖nW=\mathfrak{S}_{n}. The archetypal example of kk-transitive function on 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} is a test for the existence of a “pattern” of length kk in a permutation. For instance, a 132132-pattern of a permutation ww is any triple of increasing indices (i1,i2,i3)(i_{1},i_{2},i_{3}) such that wi1<wi3<wi2w_{i_{1}}<w_{i_{3}}<w_{i_{2}} and wi1<wi2w_{i_{1}}<w_{i_{2}}. In this light, an inversion is a 2121-pattern. More generally, for fixed kk, we can define a pattern with a permutation ρ∈𝔖k\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}, namely, a function χρ:ℕn×In,k\chi^{\rho}:\mathbb{N}^{n}\times I_{n,k} by setting

χρ​(w,(i1,i2,…,ik))={1if ​wiρ−1​(1)<wiρ−1​(2)<⋯<wiρ−1​(k)0otherwise.\chi^{\rho}(w,(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}))=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }w_{i_{\rho^{-1}(1)}}<w_{i_{\rho^{-1}(2)}}<\cdots<w_{i_{\rho^{-1}(k)}}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

If χρ​(w,p)=1\chi^{\rho}(w,\textbf{p})=1, we say that the pattern ρ\rho occurs in ww in the positions indicated by the entries in p. Then fχρ​(w)f_{\chi^{\rho}}(w) is the number of occurrences of the pattern ρ\rho in ww and gχρ​(w)g_{\chi^{\rho}}(w) is the number of occurrences of ρ\rho in adjacent positions. Hence, by Theorem 5.2, we have

(44) ∑w∈𝔖nfχρ​(w)=1k​(nk−1)​∑w∈𝔖ngχρ​(w).\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}f_{\chi^{\rho}}(w)=\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}g_{\chi^{\rho}}(w).

Here are two simple observations about any pattern ρ∈𝔖k\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}: First,

(45) χρ​(w,p)\displaystyle\chi^{\rho}(w,\textbf{p}) =χi​d​(u,p),\displaystyle=\chi^{id}(u,\textbf{p}),

where uu is the permutation obtained by rearranging letters of ww in the positions p in increasing order. Second,

(46) ∑w∈𝔖nfχρ​(w)\displaystyle\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}f_{\chi^{\rho}}(w) =n!​(nk)​1k!.\displaystyle=n!\binom{n}{k}\frac{1}{k!}\,.

For this, we can see that ℙ𝔖n​(χ1ρ=1)=1k!\mathbb{P}_{\mathfrak{S}_{n}}(\chi^{\rho}_{1}=1)=\frac{1}{k!} since there is one way to arrange the first kk letters to form the pattern ρ\rho. Since there are n!n! permutations, the claim follows from Theorem 5.2 part (a). Combining Equation 44 and Equation 46, we have

(47) ∑w∈𝔖ngχρ​(w)=(n−k+1)​n!k!=(n−k+1)!​(nk),\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}g_{\chi^{\rho}}(w)=\frac{(n-k+1)n!}{k!}=(n-k+1)!\binom{n}{k},

which can also be directly seen from Theorem 5.2 part (b).

Some classical permutation statistics can be written as sums of pattern enumerators. Let R⊆𝔖kR\subseteq\mathfrak{S}_{k}. One can see that

(48) χR≔∑ρ∈Rχρ,\chi^{R}\coloneqq\sum_{\rho\in R}\chi^{\rho},

is kk-transitive, since a permutation ww can only have a single pattern occur on a given kk-tuple of positions. Hence, from Equation 45, Equation 46, and Equation 47, we have that

(49) 𝔼⁡[fχR]=|R|⋅𝔼⁡[fχid]=|R|⋅n!​(nk)​1k!and𝔼⁡[gχR]=|R|⋅𝔼⁡[gχid]=|R|⋅(n−k+1)​n!k!.\E[f_{\chi^{R}}]=|R|\cdot\E[f_{\chi^{id}}]=|R|\cdot n!\binom{n}{k}\frac{1}{k!}\quad\text{and}\quad\E[g_{\chi^{R}}]=|R|\cdot\E[g_{\chi^{id}}]=|R|\cdot\frac{(n-k+1)n!}{k!}.
Example 5.19.

The classical peak number of a permutation ww is defined as

pk⁡(w)=|{i∈[n−2]∣wi<wi+1>wi+2}|.\operatorname{pk}(w)=|\{i\in[n-2]\mid w_{i}<w_{i+1}>w_{i+2}\}|.

Peaks of permutations are a classic topic in combinatorics and have been studied by a great many authors. See for example [1, 2, 4, 20, 58, 3, 33, 38, 39, 45, 56]. We define the horizon number of a permutation ww to be

hz⁡(w)=#⁡{1≤i1<i2<i3≤n∣wi1<wi2>wi3}.\operatorname{hz}(w)=\#\{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}\leq n\mid w_{i_{1}}<w_{i_{2}}>w_{i_{3}}\}.

Note the horizon number of a permutation is simply the number of 132132 and 231231 patterns. Namely, if R={132,231}R=\{132,231\}, then hz=fχR\operatorname{hz}=f_{\chi^{R}} and pk=gχR\operatorname{pk}=g_{\chi^{R}}. Hence,

(50) ∑w∈𝔖npk⁡(w)=2​∑w∈𝔖nfχ132=(n−2)​n!3\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\operatorname{pk}(w)=2\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}f_{\chi^{132}}=\frac{(n-2)n!}{3}

and

(51) ∑w∈𝔖nhz⁡(w)=19​(n2)​(n−2)​n!=13​(n3)​n!.\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\operatorname{hz}(w)=\frac{1}{9}\binom{n}{2}(n-2)n!=\frac{1}{3}\binom{n}{3}n!.
Remark 5.20.

Comparing Equation 37 and Equation 50 reveals that

(52) ∑w∈𝔖ndtop⁡(w)=∑w∈𝔖n+1pk⁡(w).\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\dtop(w)=\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}}\operatorname{pk}(w).

We leave finding a combinatorial proof as an open problem. See Section 6.

5.2. Generating functions

Given a family {Wn}n≥1\{W_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} of words so that Wn⊆ℤ>0nW_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{n} and WnW_{n} is 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-invariant for all nn, and given a kk-transitive function χ\chi, define the exponential generating functions

(53) F(z)=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wnfχ(w))znn!,G(z)=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wngχ(w))znn!,andH(z)=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wnχ1(w))znn!.\displaystyle F(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}f_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!},\quad G(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!},\quad\text{and}\quad H(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}\chi_{1}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}.

For example, if χ=χinv\chi=\chi^{\inv} and Wn=𝔖nW_{n}=\mathfrak{S}_{n}, then F⁡(z)F(z) is the exponential generating function for the total number of inversions, G⁡(z)G(z) is that for descents, and H⁡(z)H(z) is that for descents in the first position.

Proposition 5.21.

With F⁡(z)F(z), G⁡(z)G(z), and H⁡(z)H(z) as in Equation 53, we have the following relations:

(54) F⁡(z)\displaystyle F(z) =zk−1k!​dk−1d​zk−1​[G⁡(z)],\displaystyle=\frac{z^{k-1}}{k!}\dfrac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}[G(z)],
(55) G⁡(z)\displaystyle G(z) =z​H′​(z)−(k−1)​H​(z),\displaystyle=zH^{\prime}(z)-(k-1)H(z),
(56) dk−1d​zk−1​[G​(z)]\displaystyle\dfrac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}\left[G(z)\right] =z​dkd​zk​[H⁡(z)],and\displaystyle=z\dfrac{d^{k}}{dz^{k}}\left[H(z)\right],\text{and}
(57) F⁡(z)\displaystyle F(z) =zkk!​dkd​zk​[H⁡(z)].\displaystyle=\frac{z^{k}}{k!}\dfrac{d^{k}}{dz^{k}}\left[H(z)\right].
Proof.

These are routine computations following from Theorem 5.2. To establish Equation 54, we have

F⁡(z)=∑n≥11k​(nk−1)​(∑w∈Wngχ​(w))​znn!=zk−1k!​∑n≥1(∑w∈Wngχ​(w))​zn−k+1(n−k+1)!=zk−1k!​dk−1d​zk−1​[G⁡(z)].F(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\frac{z^{k-1}}{k!}\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n-k+1}}{(n-k+1)!}=\frac{z^{k-1}}{k!}\dfrac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}[G(z)].

Recall from Theorem 5.2(b) that 𝔼W⁡[gχ]=(n−k+1)​𝔼W​[χ1]=n​𝔼W​[χ1]−(k−1)​𝔼W​[χ1]\E_{W}[g_{\chi}]=(n-k+1)\E_{W}[\chi_{1}]=n\E_{W}[\chi_{1}]-(k-1)\E_{W}[\chi_{1}]. Hence, we have

G⁡(z)=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wngχ​(w))​znn!=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wnχ1​(w))​zn(n−1)!−(k−1)​∑n≥1(∑w∈Wnχ1​(w))​znn!,\displaystyle G(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}\chi_{1}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{(n-1)!}-(k-1)\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}\chi_{1}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!},

and therefore Equation 55 follows.

Equation 56 follows from using the product rule applied to the Equation 55. Lastly, Equation 57 follows from combining Equation 54 and Equation 56. ∎

Proposition 5.21 allows one to quickly get exponential generating functions for ∑fχ\sum f_{\chi} and ∑gχ\sum g_{\chi} given an expression for H⁡(z)H(z), which is usually the simplest to compute. Note that as far as exponential generating functions are concerned, it does not matter if one computes

G⁡(z)=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wngχ​(w))​znn!or dk−1d​zk−1​[G⁡(z)]=∑n≥1(∑w∈Wngχ​(w))​zn−k+1(n−k+1)!.G(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}\quad\text{or }\quad\dfrac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}[G(z)]=\sum_{n\geq 1}\left(\sum_{w\in W_{n}}g_{\chi}(w)\right)\frac{z^{n-k+1}}{(n-k+1)!}.

since both “record” the examined sequence in essentially the same way.

6. Future work

We conclude with some directions for further study. One can study inversions of parking functions for other variations and special subsets of parking functions, including kk-Naples parking functions, vacillating parking functions, and parking sequences and assortments. For a summary of some of these sets, refer to [6]. Thus, the program of this paper may be applied to them.

Problem 6.1.

For other families of parking functions, find nice expressions for their inversion generating functions. Furthermore, determine if there is a natural 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n}-action on the family and determine its Frobenius image.

Inversions are just one of many word statistics to consider on parking functions. Hence, one research agenda is as follows:

Problem 6.2.

Investigate generating functions for other word statistics on parking functions and their subsets and generalizations.

Next, we have seen that some qq-analogues can be explained via representation theoretic formulas. We would like fully representation theoretic explanations of all of the results in this paper. In particular, we pose the following.

Problem 6.3.

Determine the representation theoretic interpretation of Theorem 5.2 and of the equality Aninv,asc​(q,2)=UPFn⁡(q)A_{n}^{\inv,\asc}(q,2)=\UPF_{n}(q) given in Example 5.8.

Finally, in Section 5.1, our techniques have uncovered a few surprising formulas. Since our methods are purely probabilistic and/or algebraic, it would be quite interesting to find more concrete, bijective proofs of our results.

Problem 6.4.

Find combinatorial proofs of the following equations. For n≥1n\geq 1:

  1. (1)

    ∑w∈𝔖ndtop⁡(w)=∑w∈𝔖n+1pk⁡(w)\displaystyle\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\dtop(w)=\displaystyle\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}}\operatorname{pk}(w).

  2. (2)

    ∑α∈PFndes⁡(α)=∑α∈PFnfχtie​(α)\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}\des(\alpha)=\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\PF_{n}}f_{\chi^{\tie}}(\alpha).

  3. (3)

    2n​∑c⊨n∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ)=(n−1)​Fubn−1\frac{2}{n}\displaystyle\sum_{c\vDash n}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}=(n-1)\Fub_{n-1}.

  4. (4)

    ∑c∈Hess⁡(n)∑i=1ℓ(nc1,c2,…,ci−1,ci−2,2,ci+1,…,cℓ)=(n2)​(n+1)n−2\displaystyle\sum_{c\in\mathrm{Hess}(n)}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{i-1},c_{i}-2,2,c_{i+1},\dots,c_{\ell}}=\binom{n}{2}(n+1)^{n-2}.
